clinicalPearls: An autosomal recessive tubulointerstitial kidney disease and the most common genetic cause of kidney failure in children and young adults
It is a ciliopathy caused by variants in numerous NPHP genes, with a large deletion of NPHP1 being the single most frequent cause
Early features reflect impaired urinary concentration: polyuria, polydipsia, nocturia and secondary enuresis, often with salt wasting
Growth retardation and anaemia can be disproportionate to the degree of kidney impairment

Ultrasound classically shows normal or slightly reduced kidney size with increased echogenicity, loss of corticomedullary differentiation and corticomedullary cysts, distinguishing it from polycystic kidney disease with its large kidneys
Extrarenal ciliopathy features may coexist, including retinal degeneration (Senior-Loken syndrome), cerebellar vermis hypoplasia (Joubert syndrome), liver fibrosis and skeletal changes
Blood pressure is often normal until late, unlike many other progressive nephropathies
reference.pathophysiology: Nephronophthisis is an inherited ciliopathy in which variants in NPHP genes disrupt proteins (nephrocystins) that localise to the primary cilium, basal body and cell junctions of renal tubular epithelial cells. Impaired ciliary signalling and planar cell polarity disturb tubular development, cell adhesion and repair, leading to a chronic tubulointerstitial nephropathy with tubular basement membrane disruption, interstitial fibrosis and small corticomedullary cysts. Because the concentrating mechanism is affected early, the disease presents with polyuria and salt wasting before progressing to fibrosis and kidney failure. The same ciliary dysfunction in other organs accounts for the associated retinal, cerebellar, hepatic and skeletal syndromes.
additionalDifferentials: Autosomal dominant and recessive polycystic kidney disease
Medullary cystic kidney disease / autosomal dominant tubulointerstitial kidney disease
Alport syndrome and other hereditary nephropathies
additionalInvestigations: Renal ultrasound assessing kidney size, echogenicity, corticomedullary differentiation and cysts
Genetic testing including screening for the NPHP1 deletion and broader ciliopathy gene panels
Assessment of urinary concentrating ability and evidence of salt wasting
Serial kidney function and electrolyte monitoring
Ophthalmological review and, where indicated, brain imaging and liver assessment for extrarenal disease
Kidney biopsy in selected cases showing tubulointerstitial fibrosis with tubular basement membrane changes
redFlags: Progressive decline toward kidney failure requiring planning for kidney replacement therapy
Marked polyuria with dehydration and electrolyte disturbance
Visual symptoms suggesting associated retinal degeneration
Neurological signs suggesting a syndromic ciliopathy such as Joubert syndrome
reference.prognosis: Nephronophthisis is progressive and typically leads to kidney failure, with the age of onset varying by subtype (infantile, juvenile and adolescent forms); the juvenile form commonly reaches kidney failure in the teenage years. Outcome after transplantation is generally good as the disease does not recur in the graft.
pitfalls: Expecting enlarged kidneys and dismissing the diagnosis when ultrasound shows normal-sized echogenic kidneys
Missing the diagnosis in a child with unexplained polyuria, anaemia and growth failure
Failing to screen for retinal and neurological extrarenal manifestations
Attributing early salt wasting and polyuria to a primary concentrating defect without considering nephronophthisis
management: Correct the early urinary concentrating defect and salt wasting with generous fluid and sodium replacement to avoid volume depletion
Manage progressive chronic kidney disease with control of anaemia (erythropoiesis-stimulating agents and iron), renal bone disease and electrolyte disturbance
Optimise growth and nutrition, including recombinant growth hormone where growth retardation is significant
Prepare for and deliver kidney replacement therapy with dialysis and pre-emptive transplantation, which is curative for the renal disease as it does not recur in the graft
Screen for and manage extrarenal ciliopathy manifestations with ophthalmological review for retinal degeneration and assessment for hepatic fibrosis and cerebellar involvement
Refer to paediatric nephrology and clinical genetics for coordinated multidisciplinary care
Offer genetic counselling and family screening given autosomal recessive inheritance, including testing for the NPHP1 deletion
